It presents a highly readable narrative covering key figures, their contributions, shifting political circumstances, and rivalries that shaped modern go, from its early roots to the late 20th century, accompanied by representative famous games from each period and illustrations.

This online resource, described as covering "the last 400 years history of Go in Japan," likely served as a precursor to the book by compiling historical narratives in an accessible format for English-speaking audiences.

In the context of English Go literature, the work stands out for offering a cohesive narrative that integrates biographical facts, political intrigues, and representative games, providing a valuable synthesized overview where prior English materials were less centralized or thorough.

The book presents a broad historical narrative accompanied by representative games and illustrations, allowing readers to appreciate the progression of playing styles across eras with minimal commentary on individual moves.
The book provides early coverage of Go's arrival in Japan during the 8th century, noting its transmission from China to the Japanese imperial court around the Nara period.

The narrative continues into the modern era following the Meiji Restoration, examining the transition to contemporary organizations like the Nihon Ki-in, founded in 1924, and the evolution of professional Go amid broader societal changes.

A central example is the Jowa era controversies involving Honinbo Jowa and Inoue Gen'an Inseki, where the narrative explores Jowa's machinations, the bitter rivalry between the two players, and Jowa's eventual downfall amid accusations of unfair practices and manipulation in pursuit of dominance.
The minimal commentary prioritizes historical context, ensuring the games function primarily as artifacts that support the broader narrative of Go's development in Japan.

It presents the development of Go in Japan as a cohesive historical narrative rather than a dry academic text, using story-driven prose to highlight intrigue and human elements throughout the four centuries covered.

The narrative centers on political and professional dramas within the Go world, bringing the rivalries, ambitions, and personal stories of players and schools to the forefront in a compelling manner that emphasizes the human side of the game's evolution.
The narrative prioritizes contextual understanding of figures and rivalries over in-depth theoretical exploration of Go strategy.

Due to the niche nature of its subject matter, the book has attracted limited attention from mainstream literary critics, yet it remains highly valued among Go history enthusiasts for its focused historical narrative and contextual insights.

has established a lasting role as one of the primary accessible English-language introductions to the history of Go in Japan, presenting the game's development over approximately four centuries in a cohesive narrative format.

It is often referenced alongside comprehensive projects such as the GoGoD database, underscoring its enduring relevance as a supplementary narrative source despite not being the most exhaustive reference.

400 Years of Go in Japan
is a historical account of the development of the game of go in Japan, authored by Andrew Grant and John Fairbairn and published by Slate & Shell in 2004.

The work focuses particularly on the period when go rose to prominence as a major cultural art in feudal Japan, including castle games played before the shogun, and traces its evolution through professional rivalries and into the 20th century.
This book drew in part from his earlier online materials, as he previously maintained a dedicated website on the history of Go in Japan.

Grant maintained a personal website dedicated to the History of Go in Japan, which provided detailed accounts of the game's development over the last four centuries and formed the foundational material for the published work.
